A project is under way to try and help one of the UK's "most threatened" species of bumblebee.
The Bumblebee Conservation Trust is leading a Â£907,000 three-year scheme alongside the University of Cambridge to recover the Moss carder species.
It said the initiative would focus on landscapes across Cornwall's coastal grasslands, dunes and heathland as well as grazing marshes and sea walls in Kent and the upland fringe landscape of the North Pennines.
During the project, the trust said it would work with landowners to trial "small-scale habitat interventions" to identify those which work well while gaining a better understanding of the species' behaviour and needs.
Moss carder bumblebees are largely found in small, fragmented populations, according to the trust.
It said it was distinctive with a velvety covering of ginger-yellow hairs across its body and no black hairs.
The trust said habitat loss and fragmentation were likely to have a bigger impact on the Moss carder than many other species as it typically foraged closer to its nest than most other bumblebees.
Amy Plowman, head of conservation and science at the trust, said: "This is a hugely exciting and ambitious three-year project that gives us a real opportunity to turn the tide for one of the UK's rarest bumblebees."
Funding worth more than Â£530,000 has been provided to the project by Natural England's Species Recovery Programme.
Tylan Berry, Natural England's species and nature recovery networks senior officer, said the Species Recovery Programme was helping "take practical action to halt species decline and support nature recovery across England".
Berry said the Moss carder was "one of England's most threatened pollinators".
"Projects like this demonstrate how targeted investment can support practical conservation action on the ground," he added.

Iran has said it will wait for an official response from US negotiators after President Donald Trump rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within seven days.
In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but accused the president of previously making contradictory statements.
Earlier, Trump told reporters at the White House that Tehran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that they wanted to make a deal to open the strait immediately because "they're losing so badly".
On Friday at the UN, Araghchi told reporters that an agreement could be reached if "necessary conditions are met" between the two countries.
Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran that was signed in June.
Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.
The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it.
Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi said.
Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.
Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.
Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by the US ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker.
Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage".
"President Trump's right to reject it," he said.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic pressure from the US was taking a toll on Tehran.
Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.
The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran as "Operation Economic Outcast", and is using sanctions to pressure Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.
These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.
Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.
"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.
Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.
Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.
Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".
But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external
Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.
In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.
"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence.
"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."
In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.
But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.
In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.
Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her.
"Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.
Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."
Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."
'She should pay for it'
Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.
A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict.
The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.
Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.
Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.
The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.
On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.
Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution.

"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".
Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.
And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.
China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up.
"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home.
"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."
She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".
Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University â one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.
In Sinapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging.
It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.
These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times".
"Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore.
"But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it â that's how you analyse and manage it."
He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.
Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions â uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement â and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.
China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".
Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air.
"The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.
This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers.
One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."
Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."
Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."
Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.
Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."
And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.
Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.
They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.
Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.
Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly use

This investigation was reported in a collaboration between Inside Climate News and Columbia Journalism Investigations.
MCDERMITT CALDERA, Ore.—On a cold and overcast spring morning, Katie Fite stood in one of the country’s last sage-grouse strongholds, contemplating the wooden stakes in the ground that she fears warn of its destruction.
Every spring, males of the chunky bird species with spiky tail feathers come to a dwindling number of locations to strut, pop their inflatable white neck pouches and make a “paloop, paloop” sound in an attempt to court a mate. As their name suggests, sage-grouse need sagebrush, the green-brown shrub that once dominated arid Western landscapes. But both the bird and its habitat are rapidly disappearing due to climate change, invasive species, wildfires and energy development.
Now a mining company wants to extract lithium here.
Millions of sage-grouse once filled the West, but federal data shows their numbers have plummeted 80 percent since 1965 as more than a million acres of the sagebrush landscape they depend on is lost every year. They’ve long teetered toward the endangered-species list.
“We want to save sage-grouse?” Fite, public lands director for WildLands Defense, asked as she walked through the mating area, known as a lek, on the public lands where the McDermitt Lithium project would dig. “This is not how we do it. This is a travesty.”
The project’s owner agreed to avoid drilling during the sage-grouse breeding season in an effort to avoid impacting a species that is easily put off mating if conditions aren’t just right. But there is so little sagebrush habitat left in the country, Fite said, that “you can’t even pretend to mitigate this.”
Today, the U.S. has only one operating lithium mine—Albemarle’s Silver Peak in Nevada. By 2030, at least six new mining projects are predicted to be extracting lithium from American soil and another 13 will soon follow, according to a database compiled by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News. Scores more are proposed, their wooden stakes marking companies’ claims.
This element of the energy transition—lithium is used in batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage—poses stark dilemmas in the communities atop the so-called white gold. Mining it uses and displaces water, and much of it is found in water-scarce regions. Tribal nations repeatedly harmed by past extraction are disproportionately located on or near lithium-rich lands.
And then there’s vulnerable wildlife. The McDermitt Caldera’s basin is rolling hills of sagebrush and rare native wildflowers growing on strangely yellow soils in an ancient volcanic depression on the Oregon-Nevada border, its springs providing a home to threatened Lahontan cutthroat trout just as its sagebrush sustains sage-grouse. Further south in Nevada, a fully approved lithium mine, Ioneer’s Rhyolite Ridge, has faced controversy over its siting at the world’s only location of an endangered buckwheat. And scores of other proposed projects are near vulnerable species in wild, intact landscapes.
President Donald Trump is both undercutting endangered-species protections and boosting the country’s domestic mining industry, leaving plants and animals in lithium areas particularly exposed. Though the Trump administration has abandoned U.S. climate efforts and attacked the energy transition, it’s streamlining and fast-tracking permitting for lithium mines whose demand rests on that shift.
The remote McDermitt Caldera could end up home to multiple such projects.
Some of the mining claims are for projects in very early stages. But Thacker Pass, a lithium mine permitted by the first Trump administration, is under construction on the Nevada side of the caldera. The McDermitt Lithium project that would mine the lek where Fite stood is one of the first mines to be fast-tracked during the second Trump term.
All told, the Trump administration approved fast-tracking for 10 lithium mines across the country since last year. It’s doing so under a 2015 law launching the FAST-41 program that streamlines permits for large infrastructure projects. But Trump officials created an outgrowth they’re calling the “transparency program” that skips a number of requirements under the law, including coordination with local governments.
The McDermitt Lithium project tried to get into FAST-41 in 2023 but was denied by the Biden administration, according to documents from the federal agency managing the program and obtained by Inside Climate News and CJI.
The project, owned by Australian mining company Jindalee’s subsidiary HiTech Minerals Inc., is a prime example of the administration’s push to quicken mining permitting across the board. Even before McDermitt Lithium made it into FAST-41, the federal Bureau of Land Management (BLM) gave the public just five days in March 2025 to comment on the company’s proposed exploratory drilling—one of the first steps in creating a new mine.
Public backlash forced the BLM to extend the comment period to 31 days, still far shorter than usual, and the project was then added to the fast-track program to further speed its way through permitting.
In December, the BLM approved Jindalee’s plan to drill at 168 sites and build 21.5 miles of access roads across 73 of the 7,200 acres of public land the project’s site encompasses. Now, the Oregon Natural Desert Association, Great Old Broads for Wilderness and Great Basin Resource Watch are suing the BLM over its project approval, alleging the agency failed to properly evaluate the mine’s environmental impacts to species like the sage-grouse.
“When they provided at first only a five-day comment period, they were certainly making it clear that they had no interest in what the public had to say, which is certainly an indication that perhaps they’re not conducting the kind of hard-look analysis that’s required [under the country’s environmental laws],” said Ryan Houston, the executive director of the Oregon Natural Dese

On a clean summer swell, the wave at Malibu’s Surfrider Beach arrives from the south, wraps around a cobblestone point and unspools toward the pier in a long, shimmering wave that can carry a surfer for hundreds of feet. It breaks slowly, forgivingly, over rounded stones that were delivered by Malibu Creek across millennia.
The beach plays an outsized role in American and surf culture, inspiring the films “Gidget” and “The Endless Summer” and the songs of the Beach Boys. The point produced the longboarding style that still bears the place’s name: In Australia, longboards are called “Malibus.”
Kassia Meador has been reading this wave for nearly 30 years. She was 15 the summer she first paddled out at Surfrider Beach, and she has spent the decades since becoming one of the most recognizable longboarders in the world. She calls it, without hesitation, the best wave on the planet.
Lately, when Meador paddles out, something is missing beneath her: the beach. The sand at Surfrider Beach has thinned to the point where, at high tide, the ocean reaches almost to the Pacific Coast Highway. The wave itself has changed shape; the three distinct points that made Malibu’s Surfrider Beach have collapsed into one, she said. “It bunches everybody together,” she said. There’s more crowding and more tension in the water, and less of the wave that made the place worth protecting.
What’s happening at Malibu is about human intervention—a century of dams, seawalls and paved-over rivers that have starved this coastline of the sediment that builds its beaches. But it is becoming a climate story, fast, because a coast stripped of its natural defenses is a coast with nothing left to absorb what’s coming. And what’s coming this winter is a lot.
NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center has an El Niño Advisory in effect and puts the odds of a very strong event this fall and winter at greater than 90 percent—it recently broke the highest surface temperature recorded for this phenomenon, months before the projected peak. California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a statewide emergency on Monday in anticipation of heavy rainfall, high waves and flooding the phenomenon could bring.
Malibu’s First Point is one of 57 surf breaks a team of scientists, working with the conservation group Save the Waves, assessed in a study published this year in the journal Climatic Change. Their finding was blunt: Globally significant surf breaks are vulnerable to climate change, with 89 percent at medium or high risk from the loss of shoreline resilience and 79 percent from sea-level rise. Malibu made the list. But Malibu is only a single, visible instance of a reckoning unfolding along the entire California coast, where the sand that builds beaches has been cut off at nearly every source: trapped behind dams in the rivers that used to deliver it and sealed behind seawalls in the bluffs that used to shed it.
Holding Back the Sand
A beach is less a fixed place than a slow river of sand, fed by creeks and eroding bluffs and carried along the shore by waves. At Malibu, that sand and the cobble beneath it also shape the wave itself. Less sand means a thinner beach and a wave with less to stand on. To understand why the supply has dried up, you have to look inland, to a hundred-year-old dam few Californians have heard of.
Rindge Dam was built across Malibu Creek in 1926 and filled completely with sediment within about three decades—sediment that once washed down the watershed every winter and rebuilt the beach every summer. It cut the creek’s sand delivery to the coast from roughly 41,000 cubic meters a year to about 14,000.
About 780,000 cubic yards of sediment sit behind the dam today, roughly half of it sand suitable for beaches, according to California State Parks.
It is a small piece of a statewide pattern. California’s major coastal dams have trapped an estimated 152 million cubic meters of sand that would otherwise feed the state’s beaches since 1885, according to research by Gary Griggs, a coastal geologist at UC Santa Cruz who has spent five decades documenting the state’s disappearing shoreline. In Southern California, he’s found, the natural sand supply has been cut roughly in half.
Elle Overs, a marine biology Ph.D. student and a longtime Malibu surfer, sees the same mechanism everywhere she looks. “It’s a current problem that stems from a hundred years of sediment being stored up behind the Rindge Dam,” she said, and behind the concrete channels that entomb the Los Angeles and Santa Ana Rivers. “Naturally, those rivers should be bringing dirt and sand to their respective beaches.”
Further complicating the situation in Malibu is California State Parks’ 2013 restoration of the Malibu Lagoon that reconfigured the channels behind the beach to improve water quality. By most accounts, the project succeeded in doing so, but many local surfers, Meador among them, blame the project for wrecking the wave. She argues the lagoon’s mouth was never properly reset afterward, so for more than a decade it has opened toward First Point rather than at the western end of the beach, near Third Point, cutting into the sand.

California State Parks has no plan to manage the lagoon’s mouth. Its statewide policy is to let lagoons open and close naturally, said Richard Van Sant, the Rindge Dam project manager, because breaching them artificially can flush lagoon species into the ocean and kill them. Van Sant, who joined State Parks after the restoration, said he could not speak to the project itself.

Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.
Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.
In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks.
In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.
Police said thirteen men and four women were killed, adding that the motive was not clear.
In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.
No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.
The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.
Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million.
But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence.

4f2f7f8675c4.text: Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey ; Chart: Herb Scribner Cost of living and health care costs top the list of issues rural voters want 2026 midterm candidates to address, according to a new AP/KFF poll . The big picture: Ahead of the midterms, rural voters rank pocketbook concerns above immigration, the conflict with Iran and several major domestic policy debates. By the numbers: 69% of rural voters said it is 'extremely important' for candidates to talk about the cost of living, followed by health care costs (56%) and fraud in government programs (54%). Context: The AP/KFF poll asked 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas how important it was for 2026 candidates to talk about each of eight issues. Cost of living concerns Zoom in: Affordability concerns extend across a wide range of everyday expenses. 57% of rural voters cited an economic concern — including rising costs, jobs, wages and housing affordability — when asked about the biggest issue facing their local community. 67% said they were at least somewhat worried about affording gas or transportation, while 66% said the same about health care and 60% about food and groceries. Three-quarters rated the cost of living in their area as either "fair" or "poor," up 25 percentage points from 2017. Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey ; Chart: Herb Scribner Reality check: Rural voters' unhappiness with costs doesn't necessarily translate into support for Democrats. According to the poll, 40% trust Republicans more to handle the cost of living, compared with 25% who trust Democrats and 27% who trust neither party. Rural voters in the survey leaned Republican: 54% identified as GOP voters or Republican-leaning independents, while 32% identified as Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents. What we're watching: Whether economic frustration affects voter enthusiasm among rural Republicans. 27% of rural Republican voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, per the poll. Among them, 59% say they're absolutely certain to vote in the midterms. Still, 98% of rural Republicans say they're more likely to vote for a Republican than a Democrat. The fine print: The KFF/AP poll surveyed 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas nationwide from Aug. 12-24, 2026, online and by phone. The margin of sampling error is ±3 percentage points.

b0787b3e47f6.text: The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher , with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook. The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%. Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption. It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades. Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over. Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government. While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last. Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance. Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation. Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative. The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages. State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans. Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000. Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up. People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust. The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier. The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained. By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills. But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that. In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline. Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time. So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump). The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital. And that adjustment is in its early days.

Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, telling them to "maintain the greatest vigilance", ahead of a meeting with abuse survivors.
The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.
A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.
The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes, before he was scheduled to meet survivors of abuse privately later.
Before giving Mass the Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.
"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."
The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.
The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.
Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-ÃlysÃ©es Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.
On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.
During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".
The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church".
"How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.
The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.
But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.
Later on Sunday the Pope will meet staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, before taking part in a torchlight procession in the evening.
It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic church in May 2025.
Pope's have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots.

At least 10 Nepali climbers who were preparing to lead an expedition are missing after an avalanche hit a base camp in the Himalayas on Sunday.
The climb's organisers said the local guides were at a staging point close to the Himlung Himal peak in Manang district when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.
Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126 metre (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet.
Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams unable to reach the site.
Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told AFP news agency: "Eight members of our expedition team and two more from another company have been reported missing."
The Nepali team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain.
Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry.
Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches.
The latest death of Nepali climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja.
Extreme weather further south in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said.
It comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August.
More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements.

A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean.
An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back.
Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour.
Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert; they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history.
As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming.
For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia.
Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia.
The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal.
Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking.
Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio , comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community.
By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging.
The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful.
In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards.
When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours.
They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible.
Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (Â£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List.
"When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool.
"Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds.
"Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be."
Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies.
But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre.
For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live.
"They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore.
"They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me."
The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS.
And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong.
In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks.
But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise.
"Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology."
The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow.
Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years.
Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, coordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances.
Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success.
South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus.
Then came the scandals.
In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group.
Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal.
It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars.
South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement.

d38cac0d923a.text: British police said they arrested five men on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses near an air base used by the U.S. Air Force for operations in Iran . The big picture: Officials declared a major incident and set up roadblocks overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. State of play: Police received a call around 12.45 a.m. Sunday local time relating to "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be traveling towards the air base used by the U.S. 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron, per a Metropolitan Police statement . Armed officers responded and arrested the men in the Whelford area "on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act" and they were further arrested "on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act," according to the statement. Zoom in: U.K. counter-terrorism official Vicki Evans said officers established a 400-meter cordon (roughly a quarter-mile) around vehicles in the area while the British Army's Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit conducted examinations. 41d7647370b0.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/powerful-noreaster-floods-northeast-leaves-over-130000-without-power-as-high-tides-threaten-coast Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Powerful nor'easter floods Northeast, leaves over 130,000 without power as high tides threaten coast Nation Sep 27, 2026 11:15 AM EDT BOSTON (AP) — A powerful nor'easter battered the Northeast again on Sunday, flooding coastal communities and leaving tens of thousands of homes and businesses without power as forecasters warned that another round of high tides could inundate vulnerable shorelines. The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City housing authority worker when a tree fell Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf from New Jersey to New England. READ MORE: Persistent nor'easter batters U.S. Northeast, causing coastal flooding, outages and at least 1 death The storm remained just south of Long Island and east of northern New Jersey on Sunday morning and was expected to loop around the area for roughly another 24 hours, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland. The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected Sunday from northern New Jersey through New York City and Long Island into southern New England. The storm was gradually weakening, Oravec said, but the threat of tidal flooding would linger through high-tide cycles Sunday morning and again in the evening. "The most impactful parts of the storm are likely going to be the high winds and the tidal flooding," Oravec said. The nor'easter triggered memories of Superstorm Sandy, which left behind over $60 billion in damage across the eastern U.S. in 2012. While this storm's impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the East Coast this fall because of an El Niño climate pattern that's disrupting this year's weather. More than 130,000 customers were without power across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic Sunday morning, according to PowerOutage.us. The most widespread outages were along the New Jersey shore, New York's Long Island and coastal counties in Connecticut. Toppled trees across Long Island damaged homes and cars, blocked streets and downed numerous utility lines. The Federal Emergency Management Agency said response coordination centers in impacted regions were operating at an "enhanced posture," and teams were on standby in New England in case of widespread outages. On Saturday in New Jersey and New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets. Others headed to beaches to try to surf the higher-than-usual waves. Emergency crews in Sea Bright, New Jersey, rescued a woman and her dog after their vehicle became trapped in floodwaters, ABC7 reported. In Surf City, New Jersey, water rose inside a marina where workers had moved equipment to higher ground, and owner Kenny Formica said customers reported boats and Jet Skis missing or blown from their lifts. In Norfolk, Virginia, floodwaters left passing cars pushing wakes through some streets. The storm also disrupted travel throughout the region. Hundreds of flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, while flooding cut off highway access to North Carolina's Hatteras Island, stranding visitors and forcing one couple to scramble to relocate their wedding after most of their roughly 45 guests were unable to reach the island. AP journalist Julie Walker contributed from New York. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. adc6116ed831.text: By — Pan Pylas, Associated Press Pan Pylas, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/uk-police-arrest-5-men-near-an-air-base-used-by-u-s-on-suspicion-of-preparing-a-terrorist-act Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 5 men arrested near air base used by U.S. in Iran war on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act World Updated on Sep 27, 2026 11:09 AM EDT — Published on Sep 27, 2026 11:02 AM EDT LONDON (AP) — U.K. police said Sunday that five men arrested in the middle of the night near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks. London's Metropolitan Police, which takes the lead on potential terrorism activities, said local police received a call at 12:45 a.m. related to the three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that is operated by the U.S. under an agreement dating back to the Cold War. Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iran under an agreement with former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who voiced opposition to the war after it was launched by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28. The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act in the Whelford area, which backs onto RAF Fairford, which hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron. READ MORE: Trump rejects Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and other Middle East news Aerial footage from Sky News appeared to show a bomb disposal robot roaming between three white trucks. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered around. The robot appeared to be working toward getting access to the third truck. Police gave no details as to the nationality of those arrested. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be detained for up to 14 days without charge, compared to the 24-hour limit for standard arrests, without an extension application. "We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody," said Vicki Evans, the Met's counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator. "As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident." She said a 400-meter cordon has been put in place around the three vehicles that raised suspicion while the army conducts examinations. As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place. Some have been taken to a nearby recreation center. U.S. President Donald Trump heaped praise on those involved with the arrests. "It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them." The base is home to U.S. bombers striking Iran Under the terms agreed, the U.K. government allowed the American military to use Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites. His successor, Andy Burnham, is receiving updates on the situation, his office said. Iran has said the bombers flying from the base have been used for strikes beyond the original remit and indicated that a base used to attack its territory is a legitimate target. British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and sabotage attempts in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue. The arrests come at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states to the U.K., with Russia and Iran among those that have used proxies to commit crimes on their behalf on British soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states including Iran increased 50% in the six months to December 2025. Local residents evacuated as investigation continues The local Gloucestershire police force said the situation appeared to be "contained" and urged local residents to follow the advice as the investigation continues. Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said a resident had reported three "suspicious vans" in the village early Sunday. "There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there's been a major incident, said he couldn't elaborate," he said. A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said U.S. and British personnel "remain vigilant" and will take appropriate actions to ensure safety of all those at the base. "For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures," the spokesperson said. "We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families." Jill Lawless in Liverpool, England, and Ben Finley in Washington, D.C. contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 0db8ef3d6ab8.text: One day after he rejected an Iranian proposal to end the war, President Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday that he expects U.S. negotiators to engage in more talks with the country this week. Why it matters: Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, but the two sides are far apart on the key issues. While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration is demanding that Iran agree to nuclear concessions. Two regional sources confirmed Trump's comment about more talks this week. They said they expect another round of indirect dialogue between the U.S. and Iran as early as Monday. But it isn't clear if the gaps can be bridged. What he's saying: "I expect more talks with Iran [this week]. They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand," Trump said. Asked if he is considering resuming strikes against Iran, Trump said: "I am always thinking about it." State of play: In the meantime, Trump said, the U.S. military is facilitating a lot of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. He said that over the weekend the largest amount of oil transited through the strait since the war began. "More than 20 million barrels," Trump said. A U.S. defense official confirmed Trump's assertion, saying that on Friday night 22 million barrels of oil were exported through the strait. Driving the news: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last Tuesday. Qatari officials participated, passing messages between the two sides. Araghchi delivered to Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks. Iran proposed reopening the strait and restarting nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region. Trump rejected the Iranian proposal on Saturday. Behind the scenes: But a U.S. official and two regional sources told Axios that Qatari mediators are continuing shuttle diplomacy to try to reach a deal. On Thursday, the prime minister of Qatar met in New York with the Iranian president and discussed the potential deal with the Trump administration. Shortly after, senior Qatari officials met Witkoff and briefed him. A regional source with knowledge of the indirect negotiations said the Qatari mediators discussed the original Iranian proposal with both parties and provided a compromise proposal to both sides to review. What to watch: Over the weekend, the Qatari mediators have been going back and forth separately with Iranian and U.S. negotiators on changes to the text. Qatari mediators are expected to meet separately with Araghchi and Witkoff as early as Monday. The other side: Araghchi told NBC on Sunday that despite Trump's rejection of the Iranian proposal, Iran still wants a diplomatic solution. He said that the midterm elections aren't part of Iran's calculations. "We only care about our national interests. We are ready for negotiations," he said. "Although we heard from President Trump that he's rejecting this deal ... we are still waiting for an official response through the mediators," Araghchi added.

The first father and son to both be crowned champions at the Sheep Dog World Trial said they "never in million years" thought they would win the double.
Farmer David Howells and his son, Jack, 19, from Cymmer, Neath Port Talbot, travelled to the trials in Scotland last weekend.
David took the world title with his Border Collie dog, Wyverne Pip, in a field of about 300 competitors from 34 different countries.
Meanwhile his son, Jack, won the Young Handler world title with his dog, Cydros Boss.
"I feel upside down. I didn't expect to win. I can't quite believe it, to be honest," said David.
Speaking on BBC Radio Wales on Wednesday, he added it was a "crazy" experience to win alongside his son and pick up the trophies.
It marks the first time that a parent and child have won both titles at the same world trial.
"We both live on a farm, and it's a hill farm with lots of sheep, so we need the sheep dogs as every day work," he said.
"Then we've got into trials as well. To do a job that you enjoy, and then get to do a hobby alongside it, is extra special."
David said he was "proud" that his son had followed in his footsteps.
"He's grown up on the farm, and he started with the sheep dogs when he was about 10.
"During the Covid years, when he wasn't in school, he got more involved because he was home. He caught the bug, and he was mad on the sheep dogs."
The pair travelled to Lauder in Scotland over the weekend to compete, and Jack said the victory "still hasn't sunk in yet".
"It's unbelievable actually," he said.
"My mam, sister and the girlfriend all flew up to Edinburgh and came to watch. My uncle, my grandpa, were all watching from home."
David explained there were competitors from tens of countries, and that his son was in the final with two other young men from Belgium and Uruguay.
"The dog has to run up the field, picks up five sheep, and they're brought down to a set of gates," he said.
"Then, they have to drive up through a set of gates, across to another set of gates, and the sheep have to be split apart, and then they have to be put in the pen. That's the qualifying stages.
"In the final then, there's more sheep involved and it all gets a bit more technical.
"There's an element of luck involved as well because your dog's got to perform, the sheep have got to behave - they don't always. And you've got to get everything right yourself.
"So, for the two of us to achieve it, it was just extra special."
Jack said he would "stick at it" and looked forward to the International Championship next year.
"That's with the four British countries," he said.

Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality.
More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed.
The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment.
Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties.
Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia.
"People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility".
While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference".
He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace".
Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe.
This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv.
Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees.
Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s.
Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York.
Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President NicolÃ¡s Maduro.
Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.
Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure.
However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end".
Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president.
Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres.
Foro Penal confirmed the release of Miguel Castillo CedeÃ±o, who it said had been arbitrarily detained since June 2019.
Also released was Frank CabaÃ±as, who rights groups say had been held in prison for nine years after being linked to the death of a police officer. Foro Penal said he was the only suspect who remained detained, despite family members reporting that he was suffering health problems last year.
Opposition and human rights groups have said Maduro's government used the detention of political prisoners to stamp out dissent and silence critics for years.
Rodriguez has sought to frame her interim government as more permissive of political dissent while currying favour with the US. The prisoner release scheme was a key concession by her administration to the US.
However, her decision to end the scheme attracted criticism from opposition and rights groups. Foro Penal said it was stopped with less than half of the nation's political prisoners released.
Rodriguez's government continues to deny dissidents are jailed. It has cast the release of prisoners as a gesture of goodwill and reconciliation.
Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a minister closely associated with Maduro's authoritarian rule, called the interim president's meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace".
But opposition voices expressed their disapproval over the meeting, viewing it as a snub of their calls â that the US has previously endorsed â for swift elections.
Pedro Mario Burelli, a former Venezuelan state oil company executive and opposition commentator, called the two world leaders "the shameless puppet and her unscrupulous and undignified puppet-master", adding: "Little has changed in Venezuela under Washington's clumsy and selective oversight."
Venezuela's last elections, held in 2024, in which Maduro was declared the winner, were widely disputed as rigged. Opposition tallies suggested their candidate, who stood after Machado was barred from running, had won by 70% of the vote.
Despite this, the Trump administration backed Rodriguez, Maduro's former vice-president, as his successor rather than opposition leader MarÃa Corina Machado after Maduro was seized and put on trial on drug charges in January.
Analysts at the time cast this decision as the US choosing short-term stability in Venezuela until elections could be held.
Rodriguez used her UN General Assembly speech on Thursday to reiterate that there "will be elections in Venezuela", without specifying when.

23cac423bfee.text: By — Alicia León, Associated Press Alicia León, Associated Press By — Renata Brito, Associated Press Renata Brito, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/eviction-of-87-year-old-sparks-encampment-protest-in-madrid-over-housing-crisis Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Eviction of 87-year-old sparks encampment protest in Madrid over housing crisis World Sep 27, 2026 11:40 AM EDT MADRID (AP) — Protesters outraged by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman camped overnight in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza, where more demonstrators — including multigenerational families — joined them on Sunday for a second day of protests over Spain's housing crisis. Tens of thousands marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal from the apartment in the upscale Retiro neighborhood where she had lived for more than seven decades. The demonstrators are demanding stronger tenant protections, measures to combat fraud and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable. Many refused to leave after Saturday's march and pitched tents in Puerta del Sol for the night. READ MORE: Almost nowhere in California is building enough housing. Here's why "The housing situation is unsustainable," said Natalia Navarro, a 27-year-old actress who was among those camping out at the plaza. "We are all out on the street because we are fed up." "The wave of indignation and anger that has been unleashed is now unstoppable," said Alicia del Río, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union, which led the protests. "We will remain here" until the government passes new laws, including indefinite rental contracts, and stops evictions like Abascal's, del Río told journalists at the plaza on Sunday. Spain's Socialist-led government is expected to announce new measures in its weekly cabinet meeting next Tuesday. Eviction 'sparked this social unrest' On Sept. 23, Abascal was carried from her apartment on a stretcher and placed in an ambulance as supporters — who had tried unsuccessfully to stop the eviction — chanted her nickname, "Maricarmen." "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," Abascal said in a video recorded from her hospital bed after the eviction. Images of the eviction spread widely across Spain, fueling outrage and criticism of public authorities and real estate investment companies accused of pricing residents out of their homes. Critics often refer to such companies as "vulture funds." A demonstrator holds flares during a protest against Spain's housing crisis after the forceful eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her apartment in Madrid, Spain, on Sept. 26, 2026. Photo by Alejandro Martinez Velez/Reuters "Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest," said Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher who took part in Saturday's protests. Speaking at a Socialist Party rally in Madrid, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed Abascal directly: "I have a message for you, Maricarmen: the government is working around the clock to bring a Royal Decree on housing next Tuesday. And I ask parliamentary groups to make one last effort to have it validated in the National Parliament for Maricarmen." Abascal has criticized Sánchez and blamed him for her ordeal. "Does he not realize the quantity of evictions that there are daily?" she asked during an interview with Spain's state broadcaster RTVE the day before she was forcibly removed from her home. "Does he not realize, or does he not want to realize?" A home for seven decades Spanish media reported that Abascal's father first rented the apartment in 1956 and that she remained there as a tenant under rent controls after her parents died. The building changed ownership in 2018, and Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants' Union. Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros. It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros, which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said. Rising costs and a growing housing shortage Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market, despite strong economic growth in Europe's fourth-largest economy. Incomes have not kept pace with the rising housing costs, and analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply. The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share. READ MORE: Thousands protest rising housing costs in Spain's capital The demonstrations in the symbolic Madrid plaza this weekend reminded many in Spain of the historic demonstrations starting May 15, 2011, when members of the "indignados movement" camped for 28 days straight, sparking similar sit-ins across the country and the world. That movement was a reaction to evictions and other issues following a global economic crisis, including unemployment, austerity measures and corruption. Estefania Molina, a political scientist and columnist, said the stakes of popular frustration are growing. In 2011, "people protested because they couldn't buy an apartment." "Today, the protest is about not being able to rent a room in someone else's home," she told Spanish television. Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for subsidized public rental housing, which represents less than 2% of the country's housing stock. The European Union average is 8%. Brito reported from Barcelona, Spain. Associated Press journalist Suman Naishadham contributed to this report from Madrid. 5fa2a5247f4d.text: By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/swiss-reject-tighter-neutrality-rules-in-referendum-backed-by-right-wing-populist-party Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Swiss reject tighter neutrality rules in referendum backed by right-wing populist party World Sep 27, 2026 12:43 PM EDT GENEVA (AP) — Voters in Switzerland overwhelmingly rejected a proposal championed by a right-wing populist party to strengthen the country's vaunted neutrality. Supporters of the plan, led by the Swiss People's Party, which includes members with pro-Russia leanings, argued that the government had gravitated too close to the European Union and NATO, particularly over Russia's war in Ukraine. Final results from the Swiss government showed 70% of voters, and a majority in all 26 of the country's regions, rejected the plan. READ MORE: Germany's Merz faces election defeats, but no sign of leadership challenge The measure would have barred Switzerland from joining punitive measures against other countries unless they were imposed by the United Nations. Russia, one of the five permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, holds veto power over such measures. The vote was part of Sunday's latest round of Swiss referendums on local and national issues. Under Switzerland's system of direct democracy, voters typically cast ballots four times a year to help determine government policy. The proposal emerged following Switzerland's decision to join EU sanctions against Russia. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since the mid-19th century, but its meaning has been debated for years. The country is not a member of any military alliance. The proposal would have prevented the government from cooperating with an alliance — as it has with NATO for three decades — except in cases of threat. Supporters claim that the government has moved "dangerously close" to the EU and NATO in ways that threaten Switzerland's security and independence of action. Opponents argued that the federal government already has the leeway it needs to protect national interests. Security concerns influenced voters on both sides. Ruth Bolomey, a 65-year-old retiree originally from Hawaii, said she voted for the initiative. "I believe we need neutrality and should keep neutrality for security reasons — for the people." New York native Jihad Azkoul, 78, said he voted "no" and had in mind "the question of what happens if Russia attacks us — would we be, would we get protection from our neighbors?" "(They) probably would, but just to be sure," he added. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
